questions.question_text: What is the maximum speed limit for Class C airspace?
questions.correct_answer: 200 knots indicated airspeed below 2,500 feet AGL within 5 nautical miles
questions.explanation: Class C airspace has a 200 knot speed restriction for aircraft operating at or below 2,500 feet AGL within 5 nautical miles of the primary airport.

questions.question_text: What is the altitude limit for Class D airspace?
questions.correct_answer: Up to but not including 2,500 feet AGL
questions.explanation: Class D airspace is typically surface area to 2,500 feet AGL around busy airports with control towers.

questions.question_text: What is the altitude limit for Class E airspace?
questions.correct_answer: Generally from 1,200 feet AGL up to but not including 18,000 feet MSL
questions.explanation: Class E is controlled airspace; the base altitude can be higher in some areas. Above 18,000 feet MSL is Class A.

questions.question_text: What is the altitude of Class A airspace?
questions.explanation: Class A airspace begins at 18,000 feet MSL and extends upward. All aircraft require IFR clearance and transponders with Mode C.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum required cloud clearance for VFR flight in Class B airspace?
questions.explanation: Class B requires VFR pilots to remain clear of all clouds (zero cloud clearance) and have 3 statute miles visibility.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum required cloud clearance for VFR flight in Class C airspace?
questions.correct_answer: 1,000 feet above, 500 feet below, 2,000 feet horizontal
questions.explanation: Standard IFR cloud clearances apply in Class C (and Class D and E) controlled airspace.

questions.question_text: What visibility is required for VFR flight in Class B airspace?
questions.explanation: Class B requires 3 SM minimum visibility for all VFR aircraft.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum safe altitude over congested areas?
questions.correct_answer: 1,000 feet above highest obstacle within 2,000 feet horizontally
questions.explanation: 14 CFR Part 91.119 requires this altitude over congested areas.

questions.question_text: What is the minimum safe altitude over non-congested areas?
questions.explanation: Can be flown as low as 500 feet over non-congested areas, except over water/open terrain.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum altitude a private pilot can fly without supplemental oxygen?
questions.explanation: Pilots can operate up to 12,500 feet MSL without supplemental oxygen. Oxygen required above 14,000 feet MSL for more than 30 minutes.

questions.question_text: At what altitude does supplemental oxygen become required for continuous flight?
questions.explanation: All occupants require oxygen for flights at or above 14,000 feet MSL that last more than 30 minutes; above 15,000 feet MSL for all flight time.

questions.question_text: What is the standard temperature lapse rate in the troposphere?
questions.explanation: This standard is used for density altitude calculations and understanding atmospheric conditions.

questions.question_text: At what temperature do you need to correct for density altitude?
questions.correct_answer: When the temperature is 15°C (59°F) or more above the standard temperature
questions.explanation: Density altitude significantly affects aircraft performance; high temperatures and high elevations increase density altitude.

questions.question_text: What is the standard sea-level pressure?
questions.explanation: This is used as the reference for setting altimeter subscale when above 18,000 feet.

questions.question_text: What is the standard sea-level temperature?
questions.explanation: Used as reference for standard atmospheric calculations and lapse rate calculations.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum crosswind component for most general aviation aircraft?
questions.explanation: Check the aircraft's POH for specific limits; most single-engine aircraft are around 15 knots.

questions.question_text: What is the standard format for altitude clearances?
questions.correct_answer: Climb to 3,000 feet (or Descend to 2,000 feet, Level off at 5,000 feet, etc.)
questions.explanation: ATC always includes altitude restrictions in clearances; verify you understand before acknowledging.

questions.question_text: What is the standard transponder code for lost communication?
questions.explanation: Squawk 7600 if radio failure occurs; squawk 7700 for emergency.

questions.question_text: What is the transponder code for emergencies?
questions.explanation: Squawk 7700 for any emergency situation; ATC will provide priority handling.

questions.question_text: How far can you legally fly from shore in a single-engine aircraft?
questions.correct_answer: More than 50 nautical miles (gliding distance to shore required)
questions.explanation: FAR Part 91.509 requires this for single-engine aircraft; multiengine aircraft can fly further.

questions.question_text: What is the required fuel reserve for day VFR flight?
questions.explanation: You must be able to fly to your destination plus 30 minutes reserve at normal cruise power.

questions.question_text: What is the required fuel reserve for night VFR flight?
questions.explanation: Night VFR requires 45 minutes reserve beyond your destination.

questions.question_text: What is the required fuel reserve for IFR flight?
questions.correct_answer: 45 minutes at normal cruise power to alternate airport (or 30 min if forecast landing minimums)
questions.explanation: IFR pilots must have enough fuel to reach destination, then alternate airport, plus 45 minutes reserve.

questions.question_text: What is the standard rate turn?
questions.correct_answer: 3 degrees per second (360 degrees in 2 minutes)
questions.explanation: The standard rate is used in instrument flying; rate 2 is half this rate.

questions.question_text: What is the magnetic deviation tolerance for VOR equipment?
questions.explanation: VOR airborne equipment check must be within ±4 degrees; ±10 degrees for ground checks.

questions.question_text: How often must an altimeter be tested and certified?
questions.explanation: Static system and altimeter must be tested annually; encoder (Mode C) every 24 months.

questions.question_text: How often must a transponder be tested and certified?
questions.explanation: Transponder certification is required every 24 calendar months.

questions.question_text: How often must an ELT battery be replaced?
questions.correct_answer: Every 24 months or after 1 hour of accumulated transmission time
questions.explanation: ELT batteries must be replaced when this limit is reached, whichever comes first.

questions.question_text: What is the weight limit for an aircraft to be considered 'Light Sport'?
questions.explanation: Light sport aircraft have lower regulatory requirements and restrictions.

questions.question_text: What is the maximum useful load for most small general aviation aircraft?
questions.explanation: Useful load = Maximum Gross Weight - Empty Weight; must include fuel, passengers, and cargo.

questions.question_text: What G-load limits apply to normal category aircraft?
questions.explanation: Design limits for structures and stall speeds differ based on aircraft category.

questions.question_text: What is the required clearance from clouds during day VFR?
questions.correct_answer: 500 feet below, 1,000 feet above, 2,000 feet horizontal
questions.explanation: This applies to Class E airspace; Class B has stricter requirements (clear of clouds).

questions.question_text: What is true airspeed (TAS) at 5,000 feet density altitude compared to sea level?
questions.explanation: TAS increases with altitude; use flight computer to calculate exact values.

questions.question_text: How many degrees of compass error exist at the magnetic poles?
questions.explanation: Magnetic compasses are unreliable in polar regions; some areas have restrictions.

questions.question_text: What is the standard rate of descent?
questions.explanation: This is often used as a reference for normal descent; rate 2 would be 250 fpm.

questions.question_text: At what speed does a propeller become a hazard to others on the ground?
questions.correct_answer: Any rotation - always treat as a hazard
questions.explanation: Even slow propeller rotation can be dangerous; maintain clear area around aircraft.

questions.question_text: What is the legal right-of-way rule for aircraft in flight?
questions.correct_answer: Aircraft on right has right-of-way; ascending aircraft gives way to descending
questions.explanation: Know all right-of-way rules for crossing, head-on, and overtaking encounters.

questions.question_text: What is the stall speed for a 20-degree bank?
questions.correct_answer: Approximately 3% higher than level-flight stall speed
questions.explanation: Stall speed increases with bank angle; critical at high bank angles and slow speeds.

questions.question_text: At what bank angle does stall speed increase by approximately 7%?
questions.explanation: Load factor at 45 degrees is about 1.4 G; stall speed increases with square root of load factor.

questions.question_text: Cumulus clouds indicate?
questions.explanation: Fair weather cumulus = weak instability; towering cumulus = strong instability.

questions.question_text: Clear air turbulence (CAT) causes?
questions.explanation: No visual warning; common near jet streams at altitude.

questions.question_text: Lenticular clouds indicate?
questions.explanation: Severe turbulence downwind likely.

questions.question_text: Mammatus clouds indicate?
questions.correct_answer: Strong vertical instability and severe weather
questions.explanation: Pouch-like clouds; severe turbulence possible.

questions.question_text: Virga is?
questions.explanation: Often indicates severe turbulence above.

questions.question_text: Rotor clouds form from?
questions.explanation: Severe turbulence on lee side of mountains.

questions.question_text: Radiation fog forms when?
questions.correct_answer: Ground cools on clear calm night
questions.explanation: Usually dissipates by mid-morning.

questions.question_text: Advection fog forms when?
questions.correct_answer: Warm moist air over cold surface
questions.explanation: Common over water; persists for days.

questions.question_text: Orographic lifting causes?
questions.explanation: Air rises, cools, moisture condenses.

questions.question_text: Rime ice forms from?
questions.explanation: White, opaque ice; accumulates rapidly.

questions.question_text: Clear ice forms from?
questions.explanation: Heavy dense ice; most dangerous type.

questions.question_text: Carburetor icing occurs most at?
questions.explanation: Even clear skies can cause carb ice.

questions.question_text: Jet stream winds can exceed?
questions.explanation: At 35,000+ feet; affects flight planning.

questions.question_text: Freezing level approximately?
questions.explanation: Varies with temperature; icing hazard below.

questions.question_text: Stratus clouds indicate?
questions.explanation: Layered clouds; reduced visibility typical.

questions.question_text: Density altitude definition?
questions.correct_answer: Altitude where air density equals actual altitude
questions.explanation: Higher DA = reduced aircraft performance.

questions.question_text: Pressure falling rapidly indicates?
questions.explanation: Low pressure system approaching.

questions.question_text: Pressure rising rapidly indicates?
questions.explanation: High pressure system moving in.

questions.question_text: Microbursts descend from?
questions.explanation: Severe downdraft exceeding climb capability.

questions.question_text: Stall speed increases with?
questions.explanation: At 45° bank, stall speed increases ~7%.
